body:
I did another round of benchmarking with a release build and increased iteration count.

My conclusion from the data would be an improvement in call overhead with losses that stay in the margin of error. But if someone good with statistics want's to double check:

Data dump with details: [small_stack.ods](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26033507/small_stack.ods)

From a stats point of view (doing both paired t-test and "normal" t-test), this is what I get

| | 10 Args  |          |          | 2 Args   |          |          | 0 Args   |          |          |
|---------------------|----------|----------|----------|----------|----------|----------|----------|----------|----------|
|                     | Function | Inline   | Overhead | Function | Inline   | Overhead | Function | Inline   | Overhead |
| p value paired      | 1.80E-12 | 7.34E-04 | 5.47E-10 | 3.57E-02 | 2.06E-01 | 7.45E-02 | 7.62E-02 | 5.87E-01 | 8.48E-02 |
| p value two variant | 7.56E-17 | 4.12E-03 | 7.42E-13 | 2.78E-02 | 2.24E-01 | 6.08E-02 | 5.93E-02 | 5.74E-01 | 6.59E-02 |



Looks like all 3 categories of 10 args are significantly different, hence a true improvement. Their p-values are exceedingly low, and I would thus call that conclusive (well, except the inline which isn't exceedingly low, but I'd say it's low enough).
The only one that nags at me a bit is the 2-arg function, which has a p-value of 0.0357, a bit below the usual threshold of 0.05 for calling it "different". But that value isn't so low as to be enough to indicate a true difference, and thus regression, on its own.
Everything else is not statistically different per the usual threshold of 0.05 for the p-value.
